answer.sourceLine: From Democracy in America, Volume I, first published in French in 1835 as De la démocratie en Amérique — the chapter on the unlimited power of the majority (ch. XV in English; Deuxième partie, ch. VII in the French). This exact English sentence is Francis Bowen’s revision of Henry Reeve’s translation, and it is confirmed on the page ↗.

source.heading: Where the sentence actually lives

docMeta.dd: 1835, as De la démocratie en Amérique, vol. 1
Ch. XV, “Unlimited Power of the Majority in the United States, and its Consequences” — Deuxième partie, ch. VII in the French
Henry Reeve, revised by Francis Bowen (Cambridge: Sever and Francis)

source.excerpt: The authority of a king is physical, and controls the actions of men without subduing their will. But the majority possesses a power which is physical and moral at the same time, which acts upon the will as much as upon the actions, and represses not only all contest, but all controversy. I know of no country in which there is so little independence of mind and real freedom of discussion as in America. In any constitutional state in Europe, every sort of religious and political theory may be freely preached and disseminated; for there is no country in Europe so subdued by any single authority, as not to protect the man who raises his voice in the cause of truth from the consequences of his hardihood.
trail: Tocqueville wrote it in French: “Je ne connais pas de pays où il règne en général moins d’indépendance d’esprit et de véritable liberté de discussion qu’en Amérique” — in the chapter De l’omnipotence de la majorité aux États-Unis et de ses effets, confirmed in Project Gutenberg’s French text ↗.

Henry Reeve’s English translation renders the line differently: “I know no country in which there is so little true independence of mind and freedom of discussion as in America” — see Project Gutenberg’s Reeve edition ↗.

The wording everyone actually quotes comes from Francis Bowen, who revised and in great part rewrote Reeve’s translation; the scanned Cambridge (Sever and Francis) volume carries the sentence verbatim in ch. XV — Internet Archive ↗.
Wikiquote ↗ lists the sentence in its sourced section under Democracy in America, Volume I (1835), Chapter XV — not among the many lines it flags as misattributed to him.

source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the Google/Harvard scan of the Reeve translation as revised by Francis Bowen; a few obvious optical-scanning slips in the digitised text have been silently corrected against the surrounding sentences.

source.rightsNote: The French original was published in 1835, Henry Reeve’s English translation in the 1830s, and Francis Bowen’s revision of it well before 1931 — the scanned Cambridge volume carries a copyright entry dated 1862. Original text and both English renderings are therefore in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Alexis de Tocqueville
author.kicker: The traveller who took America’s temperature
author.heading: The man who came to admire American democracy — and stayed to warn about it
author.metaLine: 1805–1859 · French political philosopher, historian and deputy
author.bio: Alexis de Tocqueville was a French aristocrat and magistrate who sailed to the United States in 1831, officially to study its prisons, and came home with something far larger: Democracy in America, published in two volumes in 1835 and 1840. He admired much of what he saw — the vigour of local self-government, the habit of association, the absence of a fixed hereditary order — but he is remembered just as much for his misgivings, above all the idea that a democracy’s real danger is not a tyrant but a majority. He later sat in the Chamber of Deputies and served briefly as foreign minister, opposed Louis-Napoléon’s coup in 1851, and withdrew from public life.

misattribution.heading: Real quote, borrowed voice
misattribution.intro: Nobody has to be unmasked here — Tocqueville wrote this. What travels badly is the English it travels in, and the argument it gets cut out of.

items.why: Reeve’s own English reads “I know no country in which there is so little true independence of mind and freedom of discussion as in America” (Project Gutenberg ↗). The familiar sentence — “so little independence of mind and real freedom of discussion” — is the revision Bowen made to Reeve’s text. It is arguably the closer rendering: in the French, véritable attaches to liberté de discussion, exactly where Bowen puts “real.”

items.who: Both standard English versions, Reeve’s and Bowen’s alike
items.why: The French sentence contains the qualifier en général — “in general” — which neither translation carries over (French text ↗). Tocqueville’s claim in his own language is a shade less absolute than the one that gets quoted.

This is not a complaint about government censorship. It sits inside the chapter on the unlimited power of the majority, and the very next paragraph gives the mechanism: “In America, the majority raises formidable barriers around the liberty of opinion: within these barriers, an author may write what he pleases; but woe to him if he goes beyond them” (Internet Archive ↗). Tocqueville’s target is social pressure, not the state.

items.who: Tocqueville as an all-purpose authority on America
items.why: He is one of the most reliably faked sources in American rhetoric. Wikiquote’s Misattributed section documents the most famous example — the “America is great because she is good” sermon passage, repeated by presidents and traceable to other writers rather than to Tocqueville (Wikiquote ↗). Which is exactly why the genuine lines are worth pinning to a page.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is genuinely Tocqueville’s, from Democracy in America, Volume I (1835), ch. XV — and the English everyone recites is Francis Bowen’s revision of Henry Reeve’s translation, confirmed in the text ↗.

context.heading: Why a French aristocrat thought Americans were the least free-thinking people he had met
lead: Tocqueville had just spent nine months crossing a country that, by every institutional measure, was the freest on earth: no censor, no established church, no king. And his verdict was that Americans argued less freely than subjects of European monarchies. The reason, he thought, was structural rather than sinister. In a monarchy power is divided — a dissenter hounded by the crowd can shelter behind the throne, and one hounded by the throne can appeal to the crowd. In a democracy organised like America’s there is only one authority, and it is the majority, so a dissenter has nowhere left to stand.

What follows in the chapter is not a description of jail cells but of something more modern: the writer who steps outside the accepted range finds his career quietly closed, his allies suddenly silent, and even celebrity withheld. “The body is left free,” the same passage says, “and the soul is enslaved.” It is why this sentence keeps getting quoted — often by people who agree with each other about nothing else.
context.detailsSummary: Where the chapter sits, and why translations of it differ
detailsBody: In the standard English arrangement the chapter is titled “Unlimited Power of the Majority in the United States, and its Consequences” — Chapter XV of Volume I. In Tocqueville’s French it is the seventh chapter of the second part, De l’omnipotence de la majorité aux États-Unis et de ses effets.

Volume I appeared in 1835; a second volume followed in 1840. The book has been put into English many times, which is why the same Tocqueville sentence can look subtly different depending on which edition a quotation was copied from.
context.pull: Not a censor’s office — a room where everyone already knows what may be said.
